articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI . We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph , Denodo’s data virtualization platform , AtScale’s dimensional model , and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models . EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension . Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB. By the end of this post you will know: How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths. How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same. How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL. Three layers an agent needs An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock , the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region ). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint. The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT , row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers. Example use case: C360 on EDB Postgres AI The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit , loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view. Object Key columns customers cid , first_name , last_name , full_name , email , ssn , phone , picture , location (FK to locations.id ) locations id , city , state , zip products id , name , brand , dept , price purchases id , cid (FK to customers.cid ), pid (FK to products.id ), date , quantity , price big_spender (view) cid , full_name , state , large_orders , largest_order The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location , places purchases , and each purchase references a product. The semantic work rests on three business ideas that column names don’t reveal. State isn’t on the customer row. It lives in locations , reached through the customers.location foreign key, and a comment on that column tells SemKB where to find it. purchases.price records the order total. An agent that reads it as a unit…

articles.title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
articles.content: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue. Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication. Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions. Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments. Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line. Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM) State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech. Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include: High-quality long-range dependencies: Structured SSMs are a form of linear recurrence, but their state parameterization preserves information over long audio sequences, avoiding the long-range signal decay that limits classic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Constant memory footprint: Unlike transformers that cache all previous tokens, SSMs maintain a fixed-size hidden state. Native streaming support: The recurrent structure processes input token-by-token, so it supports true streaming without architectural modifications. These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable. How it works: SSMs for real-time voice Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription. Introducing Cartesia Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception.…

articles.title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
articles.content: Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release. In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production: “Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.” — Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish. Choose where inference can run Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles . You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions. Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure. The inference profile ID you invoke controls which destination Regions are eligible: Profile Model ID When to choose it Global global.moonshotai.kimi-k3 Recommended for most use cases: lowest cost and most broadly available India geographic in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 Inference processing must stay within Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions See the Amazon Bedrock Kimi K3 model card for up-to-date information on available inference profiles, which AWS Regions they can be called from, and what destination Regions they can use for inference. Example walkthrough: Indic-language document understanding Let’s consider an example use case: reading a scanned Hindi document, extracting structured data, and answering follow-up questions in mixed Hindi and English (Hinglish). This need is common in Indian financial services and public sector workflows where know your customer (KYC) forms, utility bills, and similar documents must often be digitized. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock can directly read and reason about images, including those containing multilingual text. It offers a potential solution with no separate OCR or translation service required. Prerequisites The full source code for this example is available on GitHub . To follow along, you need: An AWS account . Python 3.11 or later installed, with internet access to install the required PyPI packages . The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed, with credentials configured with sufficient AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to invoke the Kimi K3 model through the India inference profile. For example, to use Kimi K3 through the ap-south-1 Mumbai Region with India geographic inference, the following IAM policy grants sufficient access. Replace the {ACCOUNT_ID} placeholders with your AWS account ID: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "BedrockCallWithBearerToken", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:CallWithBearerToken"], "Resource": ["*"] }, { "Sid": "BedrockKimiK3India", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-south-1::foundation-model/moonshotai.kimi-k3", "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-south-2::foundation-model/moonshotai.kimi-k3",…

articles.title: Athena Raises $2.5 Million From a16z Speedrun to End the Billable Hour in Real Estate Law
articles.content: American law firms bill an estimated $403.9 billion a year , most of it by the hour, at rates that now reach about $3,400 an hour for a top partner at a large firm, more than double the top rate of a decade ago. Investors have spent the past 18 months pouring money into the software side of that market, with Legora valued at $8.8 billion and Harvey at $15.6 billion , yet the two together still bill only about 0.1% of what law firms earn. The bigger prize is the legal work itself, which is where a new group of AI-native law firms that sell finished work at fixed prices has raised at least $111 million in 13 months (our calculation). Commercial real estate is one of the busiest places to compete for that work, since about $2.5 trillion of US commercial mortgages fall due between 2025 and 2027 (our arithmetic) and every refinancing or sale needs loan documents, diligence and a closing. Athena , an AI-native legal service for commercial real estate investors founded by former Legora staff, raised a $2.5 million pre-seed round on 3 November 2026 led by a16z Speedrun , the Andreessen Horowitz accelerator that admitted fewer than 0.4% of applicants into its latest cohort. In the two months since launch the San Francisco company has signed 22 clients at fixed fees that typically run 30% to 50% below what those clients paid on recent deals, while its mix of AI agents and attorneys cut review time by more than 70% in the first six weeks. Legal Services and Legal AI in 2026 Law firm revenue has grown only about 1.4% a year over the past five years to an estimated $403.9 billion in 2025, which leaves room for a faster and cheaper model to take share. The two largest legal AI companies sell software into that market, with Harvey's annual recurring revenue above $400 million and Legora growing from $1 million to $100 million in under 18 months, a scale that still leaves both far smaller than the firms they sell to and shows how much larger the market for finished legal work is than the market for legal software. Investors are paying up for the companies leading the software side. Legora, where Athena's founders met, raised a $550 million Series E at an $8.8 billion valuation on 21 October 2026, about 13 times the roughly $675 million it was valued at in May 2025 (our arithmetic). Harvey raised $550 million at $15.6 billion in September, which puts the two at $24.4 billion combined. Legora's reported rounds add up to about $1.4 billion raised to date (our arithmetic), which gives its alumni a close view of what law firms will and will not change once AI arrives. The Billable Hour Nightmare and Big Law Most of that $403.9 billion is still billed by the hour, at rates that keep climbing. A top partner at a large US firm now charges about $3,400 an hour , more than double the roughly $1,500 that drew criticism about a decade ago, while partner rates at the 50 largest firms rose 16% on average over the past year and Susman Godfrey's top partners moved from $3,000 to $4,000 an hour for 2026. Across the wider market, average partner rates rose 5.1% in 2025 , the joint second-largest rise since its tracking began in 2013, while firms with more than 750 lawyers handled 52% of matters. articles.title: South Korea Wants Stablecoins Written Into Its Forex Law Within The Year
articles.content: The Bank of Korea plans to prepare the bill jointly with the government before the year ends. Unhosted wallets and mixers are already on its radar. South Korea is moving on two tracks at once. The first is fast and narrow. The government and the Bank of Korea plan to revise the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act this year, so that stablecoins are regulated as payment instruments. The second is slow and broad: the Digital Asset Basic Act , a comprehensive framework that the government is still developing. The forex amendment is how the central bank intends to act before that larger law arrives. A payment instrument, by statute The Bank of Korea said it is coordinating with the government on measures to regulate cross-border transactions in digital assets. Its stated plan has two parts: A bill, prepared jointly with the government within this year , amending the forex law to regulate stablecoins as a means of payment A monitoring framework for virtual assets , prepared alongside that bill Note the vehicle. The change runs through the forex law, ahead of the dedicated digital asset law still in development. The audit that set this in motion The plan answers last year's National Assembly audit. During that audit, lawmakers asked the Bank of Korea to bring local payment infrastructure up to global standards. Two requests are on the record: Extending the operating hours of large-value payment systems to 8 p.m. Establishing measures to prevent money laundering risks linked to the entry of global crypto exchanges Unhosted wallets, in the central bank's own words The Bank of Korea also said it would focus on building an international cooperation framework to combat illegal digital asset transactions . Its reasoning is worth reading closely. In the central bank's view, these transactions enable cross-border transfers outside traditional financial institutions. It added that tools like mixers and unhosted wallets increase anonymity, which makes illicit activities easier to carry out. This is the central bank's stated view, not yet a rule. But it shows which tools the institution drafting the forex amendment is watching. For anyone holding their own keys, that is the part of this story to follow as the bill takes shape. The bigger bill is almost ready The Digital Asset Basic Act seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for crypto, including: Licensing regimes for exchanges Rules for stablecoin issuance On Thursday, at a hearing, Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission, said discussions on the bill were nearing completion. He said the government will work to introduce it as soon as possible. Until then, there is a gap. The Bank of Korea said it will continue consulting with relevant ministries to minimize regulatory arbitrage that could arise from temporary legislative gaps while the Digital Asset Basic Act takes shape. What we know so far Who: the South Korean government and the Bank of Korea What: an amendment to the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act regulating stablecoins as payment instruments, plus a monitoring framework for virtual assets When: a bill to be jointly prepared within this year Why: last year's National Assembly audit, which asked for 8 p.m. operating hours for large-value payment systems and anti-money laundering measures tied to global crypto exchanges Next: the Digital Asset Basic Act, with exchange licensing and stablecoin issuance rules, which the Financial Services Commission chairman says is nearing completion The big picture South Korea is not waiting for its comprehensive law to define stablecoins. It is reaching for the statute it already has, the forex law, and framing stablecoins as a payment and cross-border issue first. The pattern is clear in the central bank's own words. Cross-border flows outside traditional institutions come first, and mixers and unhosted wallets are named in the same breath as illicit activity. The Digital Asset Basic Act will set the broad rules. articles.title: Password manager mSecure tells users to change passwords, won't say why
articles.content: Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register , US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously. "Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys." For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace. The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers. "Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised." Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved. "I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked. A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself. The confusion has also spilled onto Reddit , where customers have shared copies of the vague notification and questioned what might have happened. mSeven has yet to respond to The Register 's questions, leaving customers to guess whether their data has actually been compromised or the company is simply being cautious. That's not exactly reassuring from a business whose entire purpose is keeping other people's secrets safe. The company's email concludes: "We regret any inconvenience that this may cause." For customers contemplating hundreds of password resets, "inconvenience" may be putting it mildly. ®

articles.title: Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed
articles.content: Microsoft’s Dona Sarkar (left) looks on as members of the FROM YOUR EYES team hoist the trophy after winning the 2024 Imagine Cup at Microsoft Build in Seattle. The competition is expanding beyond students for the first time in 2027. (GeekWire Photo / Todd Bishop) Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner. The change, announced Monday , opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students. Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories. It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era. Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services. For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud. The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services. Microsoft Foundry , the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models. Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups. (Microsoft Photo) “Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions. Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses. The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers. As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted. What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. articles.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
articles.content: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational. Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim? UEFI bootkit refresher Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface , UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS. Read full article Comments

articles.title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
articles.content: Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers. Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing. Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress. Using the NVIDIA cuDSS library, multiphysics software provider COMSOL is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically. Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster. In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating NVIDIA cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print. As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes. Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time. The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware. Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time. Applied Materials uses digital twins built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to simulate fab-level optimizations in layout, throughput, cost and process control. articles.title: Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
articles.content: Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it. I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with. Louis The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker. A community that brings its own ideas When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed. Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own. The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project. Louis How a trash bin gets into Minecraft Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds. Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type. If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks. One maintainer, a stack of pull requests As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day. He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased. I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it. Louis Sub-agents that look for regressions Big features arrive as big pull requests. Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time. articles.title: MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from VentureBeat: Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) reported today that they used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra language model to raise a small, open source Qwen model's math score roughly sixfold by directly editing its weights -- the numerical parameters that govern its behavior. Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab described their work in a research blog post published November 2. They call the approach "weight-space programming" and tested Astra's ability to interpret and alter networks without using conventional training procedures to generate the edits. In the strongest language-model example, Astra's intervention raised Qwen3.5-0.8B's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% while touching approximately 0.016% of its weights. The improvement came primarily from correcting repetitive reasoning—a distinction that shaped both the technical findings and the debate over their implications. Their experiments explored a broader possibility: AI systems that inspect, repair and construct other neural networks by working directly on their internal machinery. "This is cool as heck!" wrote Yuchen Jin, a technical staffer at Databricks and former co-founder and CTO of Hyperbolic Labs who was unaffiliated with the research, on X. "Imagine using a large LLM to directly edit a smaller model's weights and dramatically improve its capabilities. It's like gene editing for neural networks. Even cooler than distillation!" Voyage AI staff researcher Chandan Singh, formerly of Microsoft AI, also reacted to the findings: "For anyone questioning whether this post is overhyped, I think they are actually *underselling* the approach." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: OpenAI introduces program to reduce AI data center energy demand during peak hours
articles.content: Electricity consumption is one of the biggest concerns that residents bring up whenever a data center is proposed in their community, which is why OpenAI is taking steps to minimize its impact on the local electricity grid. According to the company , its Grid Protectors Program aims to reduce the power consumption of its data centers as local demand increases, ensuring that the grid is not overwhelmed during peak hours. Aside from ensuring that the lights remain on for everyone, it would also allow its data centers to connect to the grid and go online sooner instead of waiting for the additional power sources to come online. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible “Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most,” OpenAI said in its blog. It also added, “Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.” OpenAI is testing the program in its planned Effingham County campus in Georgia, with the company saying that it has already signed a 3.2-gigawatt agreement with Georgia Power that included 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. This ensures that if demand jumps on the hottest days of the year, there would be enough power to accommodate the hundreds of thousands of air conditioners keeping Georgians cool. With the average American home drawing around 1,200 kilowatts, the 1,000-megawatt buffer is more than enough to power around 800,000 households — nearly 20% of the state’s homes. This technology, called demand response, has been around for decades now, where large operators reduce their demand in response to a peak in demand from other consumers. Before automation, grid operators would manually call up industrial customers like steel mills and ask them to cut consumption to ensure the reliability of the entire grid. But with modern technologies and IoT, it can now be done automatically, allowing data centers to reduce their load in under a minute. In fact, Nvidia has already been experimenting with a similar system in the UK and has proven that it works.

articles.title: iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8: Is $2,000 worth it?
articles.content: How much would you pay for a phone that turns into a small tablet? Apple is betting the answer is nearly $2,000. After seven years of watching Samsung build folding phones, Apple has finally entered the race with its first-ever foldable iPhone. The new iPhone Duo, which went on sale Oct. 23, opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Its biggest competitor, Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 , offers the same screen size and a remarkably similar design. However, Samsung's phone is lighter and costs about $100 less. Apple has some interesting advantages of its own, including impressive battery performance and a clever screen designed to reduce glare. But there are compromises on both sides, including a repair bill that might make you think twice about carrying either phone without protection. So, has Apple finally cracked the folding phone formula, or does Samsung still have the better idea? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Samsung introduced the original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Those early devices came with plenty of growing pains, including concerns about screen durability. Since then, Samsung has steadily improved its folding technology. Apple took its time. In fact, we covered one of the company's early ideas in our article about Apple's foldable iPhone patent in 2023. Now the iPhone Duo is finally here, and Apple has made some interesting design decisions. The phone features a polished titanium frame, Apple's A20 Pro processor and a large inner OLED display. It also introduces a redesigned version of iOS built around the folding experience. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes a different approach. It uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and Samsung's One UI 9 software, which has evolved through several generations of folding phones. That experience gives Samsung an advantage in some areas. However, Apple has already managed to outperform its rival in early battery testing. Let's get the painful part out of the way. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. The 512GB model costs $2,199, while the 1TB version jumps to $2,599. If you really want to splurge, Apple's 2TB model costs an eye-watering $3,199. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99 for 256GB. The 512GB version costs $2,099.99, while the 1TB model reaches $2,499.99. That puts Samsung roughly $100 below Apple at comparable storage levels. Of course, Samsung has another advantage. Its Fold 8 has been on sale since August, so retailers and carriers have had time to introduce promotions. However, I'd look closely at those deals before celebrating the savings. Some carrier offers require a qualifying trade-in or a lengthy commitment to monthly bill credits. There's also a larger question. When you're already spending nearly $2,000, will saving $100 really determine which phone you choose? I suspect the answer comes down to what happens when you actually hold them. One of the first things you'll notice about these phones is how similar they look. Both fold horizontally like a book, with smaller screens on the outside and expansive displays when opened. But there's a noticeable difference in weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 8.96 ounces, compared with 7.09 ounces for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's almost two ounces heavier for Apple's phone. If you've ever carried a heavy smartphone in your pocket all day, you know how noticeable that can become. The difference could be even more…

articles.title: How We Stabilized a Bazel CI Runner by Fixing Resource Limits and Container Cleanup
articles.content: It all started as a routing investigation. The monorepo (Go, nodejs, C++ with shared proto files) pipeline had been running slowly for some time, and then it started to fail. Bazel builds were being OOM-killed during working hours, the retries lengthened the queue, the longer queue reduced the frequency of pushes, and the CI issues quietly escalated into engineering problems. Upon finally logging into the runner host, I found that the machine, with 6 cores and 12 threads, had a load average of 32.7. Swap space was being used. There was nothing wrong with the box in the conventional sense. It was working exactly as instructed, but the instructions themselves were bizarre. The cause was a comment in the .bazelrc file describing a different machine. The CI configuration block briefly stated that the runner could run a maximum of two Bazel containers simultaneously, and therefore each build could consume five CPU threads and 24 GiB of memory. The calculation was correct for the target runner at the time it was written. However, the two CI tags used in the monorepo had been resolving to a different runner for quite some time, and that other runner was set to concurrent=10 with no per-job restrictions whatsoever. In other words, the machine with 6 cores and 62 GiB of memory was accepting 9 jobs at once, and each Bazel job among them was requesting the budget promised in the comment. In total, the containers on that host perceived themselves as having 25 CPUs and 120 GiB of memory. There were no cgroup limits that dictated anything else. The only restriction in the whole system was Bazel's own local_resources setting, but this setting is an estimate for the Bazel scheduler, not a hard limit. This fix was intentionally boring and required three days of readjustment to get it working correctly. First, a hard cgroup limit was imposed on the runner, allowing three jobs with four CPUs and 14 GiB of capacity each to run simultaneously. Next, we ran four jobs using four CPUs and 12 GiB. After that, we ran five jobs using three CPUs and 11 GiB, at which point the processing stabilized. Then, with each step, .bazelrc gradually decreased from 5 CPUs and 24 GiB per build to the following: # CPU: 3 threads (5 x 3 = 15, 1.25x SMT) # RAM: 9GiB under the 11GiB cap. Measured peak per job was 11.37GiB working # set but only 6.68GiB RSS, the rest reclaimable page cache # Jobs: 5, deliberately above the CPU budget so sub-CPU actions still fill it build:ci --local_resources=cpu=3 build:ci --local_resources=memory=9216 build:ci --jobs=5 Two of the rules within that block took me an egregious amount of time to understand. The value of local_resources must be strictly below the upper limit of cgroup. This is because if there is a margin, resource-intensive processes will be queued instead of being OOM-killed. Furthermore, the memory value should be determined based on the actually measured 6.68 GiB resident memory set, not on the 11.37 GiB working set. This is because the difference between these two values represents the reclaimable page cache that the kernel frees when needed. There was another surprise on the CPU side. The first version of the caps used a hard CFS quota, so the box quickly went into half-idle mode. Measurements revealed that host utilization was only 50%, and the one job actually running was throttled in 93% of its CFS periods. Hard quotas serve to protect neighbors that don't yet exist, but this is achieved by tightening the limits on currently running jobs. Therefore, while the CPU limit was no longer strictly defined and a fair allocation method was adopted, the memory limit was strictly maintained. This is because memory is the resource that actually kills. Additionally , some jobs were moved. The Starlark linter and code review helper were occupying build slots on the loaded runner, but since linters shouldn't occupy build slots, both were moved to a lighter runner. The only remaining process was the computation of the affected…

articles.title: Intel 14A moves closer to production as PDK 0.9 becomes available
articles.content: Intel Foundry last week made available its Intel 14A process design kit (PDK) version 0.9, an important milestone in the development of this next-generation manufacturing technology. The company says that the production node is reaching performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, and the results are backed by silicon validation. Intel plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027, which will validate the technology's readiness for high-volume manufacturing (HVM). Go deeper with TH Premium: Chipmaking (Image credit: tsmc) Analyzing TSMC's fab expansion roadmap — multi-fab N2 ramp, CoWoS, SoIC, and uncorking bottlenecks Leading-edge foundry roadmaps for TSMC, Intel, and Samsung ASML's roadmap for chipmaking lithography tools examined Chinese chipmaking tool roadmaps examined 14A PDK v0.9 is here A process design kit contains transistor models, design rules, and other information that enables chip designers to develop products for a particular manufacturing process using electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The accuracy and quality of the PDK are crucial for modelling how chips will perform once manufactured, and the release of PDK 0.9 is particularly important because it provides customers with a representation of Intel 14A based on actual silicon measurements rather than on theoretical models or simulations. At this stage, customers can proceed with product development with greater confidence that the technology will meet their requirements when it comes to performance and power consumption. (Image credit: Intel/Tom's Hardware) Intel says that PDK 0.9 lets customers develop designs intended to enter risk production around the time the process is certified, which — provided that PDK accurately reflects the characteristics of manufactured silicon — in many cases enables chip developers to greatly reduce the number of silicon revisions between initial tapeout and mass production. Of course, availability of PDK 0.9 does not indicate that Intel 14A is ready or even close to mass production, as the company expects to validate HVM readiness only with PDK 1.0, sometime in Q1 2027. Again, this does not mean that 14A will enter mass production in early 2027, as Intel itself expects to begin mass production using its 14A process technology in 2028, following risk production for its own products in the second half of 2027. "From a customer perspective, the PDK 0.9 gives customers the confidence to design products on Intel 14A, as the technology is reaching the industry-standard performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, supported by silicon-backed validation," said Ben Sell, corporate vice president and general manager of front-end technology development at Intel Foundry. Building on top of 18A Intel 14A builds on top of architectural foundations introduced with Intel 18A but incorporates several substantial enhancements. These include 2 nd Generation RibbonFET 2 gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, PowerDirect backside power delivery (which delivers power right to the transistor source/drain regions without using intermediate connections like TSVs used by PowerVia), and Turbo Cells (high-performance standard cells designed to accelerate timing-critical paths in CPUs and GPUs), which provide chip designers with additional ways to increase performance and optimize power efficiency. Since Intel has previously outlined advantages of these technologies, the latest announcement does not provide updates regarding transistor performance, power consumption, or transistor density figures for Intel 14A. Beyond improvements to transistor, power delivery, and interconnect technologies, Intel is applying manufacturing experience gained during 12 months of Intel 18A production to accelerate maturation of 14A. Specifically, the company says it has increased investments in inline defect detection, modeling, and simulation to identify potential manufacturing problems earlier in the…

articles.title: How I Used a Stock Market Theory to Predict Cellular Network Behavior
articles.content: The strangest paper I have ever written started with a stock chart. In 2016, I was working on handoff prediction for cellular networks, the problem of anticipating when a moving phone should jump from one base station to the next. Get it right and the call continues seamlessly. Get it wrong and the call drops, the video buffers, the user curses the carrier. The standard tools were signal-strength thresholds and mobility models, and they all shared a weakness: they reacted to the network instead of anticipating it. Around the same time, I found myself reading about Elliott wave theory. If you have never encountered it, here is the sixty-second version. In the 1930s, an accountant named Ralph Nelson Elliott noticed that stock market prices do not move randomly. They move in repetitive wave patterns, five waves forward, three waves back, driven by the collective psychology of crowds swinging between optimism and pessimism. The patterns repeat at every timescale, from minutes to decades. Traders have argued about its predictive power ever since, but the core observation is hard to dismiss: human crowds generate structure, and that structure rhymes. And then the thought that would not leave me alone: crowds also move through cities in waves. Think about it. Morning commute, lunch hour, evening rush, stadium emptying after a match. Thousands of phones crossing cell boundaries in rhythmic, quasi-periodic surges. The handoff load at a base station is not random noise. It is crowd behavior rendered in signaling traffic, and crowd behavior has patterns. If Elliott's waves could describe the mood swings of markets, why could they not describe the movement swings of a city? I brought the idea to my colleagues, and I will be honest: the first reaction was the one you are probably having now. What does the stock market have to do with cell towers? Fair question. But strip away the finance vocabulary and Elliott wave theory is really a claim about self-similar patterns in time series generated by collective human behavior. Network signaling traffic is exactly that kind of time series. The domain changes; the mathematics of waves does not care. We built a handoff prediction method around wave-pattern analysis of network traffic. Instead of waiting for a signal threshold to trip, the approach looks for the rhythmic structure in boundary-crossing activity and projects it forward, the way a surfer reads a swell rather than reacting to the water already under the board. The work went through peer review and was published in 2016 as ' Experimental Study on Elliott Wave Theory for Handoff Prediction ' in Fluctuation and Noise Letters — which in this field means it survived the scrutiny of reviewers who were at least as skeptical as you are. Did it beat every conventional method on every metric? No, and I will not claim that. What it did was demonstrate something I find more valuable: a completely foreign mathematical framework, imported from finance, could say something true about wireless networks. The patterns held. The predictions worked well enough to stand alongside established approaches, and in bursty, crowd-driven scenarios, the wave structure captured dynamics that threshold methods missed entirely. Here is the part I actually want you to take away, because it is bigger than one paper. Engineering education trains us to go deep. Pick a lane, master its tools, publish in its journals. Depth matters enormously. But some of the best ideas I have encountered in twenty years of research came from sideways reading. Antenna designers who studied optics. Signal processing borrowed from seismology. And yes, handoff prediction borrowed from a stock-market accountant in the 1930s. The mechanism is simple. Every field develops blind spots, assumptions so baked in that nobody questions them. Wireless engineers assumed handoffs were best predicted from radio measurements, because handoffs are radio events. That assumption was not wrong, but it was…

articles.title: Flip Phones, AI Hype, and Smart Glasses: What Readers Want Control Over
articles.content: Hey Hackers! Welcome back to 3 Tech Polls , HackerNoon's Monthly Newsletter that curates Results from our Polls of the Week . Today, we look at four polls: we handed you a genie, a boss, a bubble, and a pair of camera glasses. You told us which piece of old tech deserves a comeback, how your workplace really handles AI, what it would take to prove the boom isn’t hype, and whether smart glasses belong in public—the verdict: a little nostalgic, but a whole lot skeptical. Let’s dig in 🔥 The Genie Poll: What Should Come Back Forever? Offered one resurrection, most readers reached for something they could hold. Flip phones (40%) and the iPod click wheel (21%) took 61% of the vote between them. The three platforms, Flappy Bird, Vine, and MySpace, had more spots on the ballot and still totaled only 33% . The genie’s fine print may explain it: a device comes back working on day one, while a platform comes back empty, minus the people who made it worth opening. The remaining 6% wrote in their own answers, and one stood out. A reader picked Yahoo 360, a platform, for a personal reason: it’s where their teen blogs vanished. Even the exception isn’t asking for a feed. It’s asking for something that was once theirs. Is Your Boss Okay With AI? On paper, AI at work looks settled. Of 86 voters, 88% have a green light: 57% are fully encouraged and 31% are limited to approved tools. Another 9% say their boss “doesn’t care as long as the work is done.” But a green light isn’t the same as oversight. A separate PagerDuty/Wakefield survey of 1,250 non-IT office staff at companies with $500M+ in revenue found 66% of office professionals have used AI tools they believed weren’t permitted (PagerDuty, 2026). Different crowd, so it can’t tell us what our readers do, but it shows how easily the rulebook and real behavior drift apart. That’s why the 9% might be the most candid answer here. In some teams, the real AI policy is just the deadline. What Would Prove the AI Boom Isn't Hype? Ask readers what would prove the AI boom is real, and the biggest bloc reaches for a calculator. Of 49 voters, nearly half (49%) defined proof in financial terms: consistent profits (29%) , less investor dependence (12%) , and lower costs (8%) . Productivity and adoption together drew only 30%. That sits awkwardly next to our boss poll, where most voters said they’re encouraged to use AI at work. Different voters, so call it a tension rather than a contradiction, but it’s a telling one: you can use AI daily and still doubt the economics. Professional investors share the split. In BCG’s survey, 87% expect AI to materially improve corporate fundamentals, yet 56% say the market is too optimistic on AI (BCG, 2026). Believing in the tech and believing in the price tag are two different bets. Should AI Glasses Be Banned in Public Spaces? The safeguard the industry leans on hardest finished dead last. Only 5% of 64 voters think clear recording signals, like the small light on camera glasses, are enough. Meanwhile, 63% want some form of restriction, and 25% say existing laws should cover it. Those are different answers, since one asks for new rules and the other would rather apply laws already on the books, but they agree on one thing: 88% want the law doing the work, not a status light. Norway’s proposal covers selected places, not a blanket ban (Reuters, 2026), and it’s temporary, though the list is long: parks, beaches, schools, shopping centers. The Irish Times calls Norway the “first major country to propose” this kind of ban. Whether readers want more than that depends on what “some restriction” means to them. What they clearly don’t want is to rely on a light. So, What Did We Learn? Four polls, four different groups of voters, but the same instinct shows up in all of them. Asked to bring something back, readers would rather revive a gadget they could hold than a platform that’s lost its crowd. Most have the green light to use AI at work, but they know the rulebook and the…

articles.title: AI Agent Memory (Part 3): How Agents Turn Experience Into Reusable Skills
articles.content: An agent can form the wrong lesson, then fix it after another correction. But what if it keeps making the same kind of mistake when forming new lessons? Updating a Skill can fix one task. The bigger change is improving how the agent turns the next experience into something worth learning. This time, it remembered The second article in this series asked why an agent might miss a saved lesson. This time, it finds the note and follows it. The trouble starts earlier: what lesson did it form from the experience? Imagine asking for a quick update before a team meeting. The agent writes several pages. You say, “This report is too long.” It saves: “The user prefers short reports.” Later, you need a report to decide whether to spend money. The agent keeps it short, leaving out the evidence you need. It remembered your words. But did it understand what they meant? One comment can mean different things Maybe you prefer short reports. Or maybe that meeting only needed a quick update. Both explanations make sense. One comment is not enough to settle it. A belief is what we currently think is true. It shapes what we expect and do. If the agent believes you dislike detail, it will keep cutting detail. If it thinks the problem was specific to that meeting, it should check what the next report is for. The event is evidence. The lesson is an interpretation of that evidence. Now you ask for more evidence. Should it flip to “the user likes long reports”? That would repeat the same mistake with a different answer. From experience to a Skill There are three useful stages to picture here: Keep the event and its setting. What happened, and what were we trying to do? Find a possible pattern. Perhaps the amount of detail depends on the report's purpose. Turn it into a method. Check the purpose before deciding what to include. Each step involves judgment. A shorter record can lose the setting. A pattern can stretch beyond the evidence. A method can turn a useful idea into an overly broad rule. Agents already do parts of this. Hermes , an open-source agent, can create and edit Skills : reusable instructions, sometimes with scripts and supporting files. EvoMap's GEP protocol also describes strategies with conditions, checks, and outcome records that can guide later choices. So the question goes beyond whether an agent can write or revise a useful procedure. It can. The question is what the revision changes. Fix this lesson—or how the next one is formed? The report-writing Skill could now say: Keep meeting updates brief. Include enough evidence for spending decisions. That fixes the lesson. But next week, you ask for one email to sound less formal. Will it save “the user always prefers casual writing”? If so, the report rule improved, but the same mistake survived: turning one request into a lasting preference. There are two places the result can feed back into: The lesson itself: change the rule about report length. The way lessons are formed: reconsider how the system separates a one-time request from a lasting preference. We can add an instruction: “Do not save a permanent preference from one request.” That can help. But the system still has to decide what counts as enough evidence and when an exception matters. If later results help revise that decision process, the feedback reaches further. If they only rewrite individual Skills, the system can keep repairing lessons while repeating the same mistake in how it creates them. The agent updates the lesson. What updates how it forms the next one? What people can learn beyond the rule After a few misunderstandings like this, a person may stop taking every comment as a general rule. They start asking what the other person needed in that situation. That change can involve four abilities: Notice the setting. A quick update and a spending decision need different evidence. Limit the conclusion. One request does not tell you what someone always wants. Revise a belief. New evidence can refine an explanation…

articles.title: 8 converted jet engines are powering xAI data centers as companies look for new energy sources
articles.content: Elon Musk's xAI is using eight converted jet engine turbines to power a Mississippi data center. While the generators have the required state-level permission and permits, there remain concerns about the impact they could have on the local environment. The permits allow for a 25% higher limit in pollutants known as volatile organic compounds, but those compounds, paired with the expulsion of carbon monoxide, have environmentalists warning that the use of jet engines to power data centers is a step in the wrong direction. The New York Times reports that the Southern Environmental Law Center has already challenged Mississippi's decision to approve the turbines for use at xAI's data center. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The group argues that xAI has failed to provide guarantees that the jet-powered turbines meet emissions standards for specific pollutants, including formaldehyde. It also accuses xAI of what the report terms the "undercounting" of projected emissions in relation to the data center's power sources. This comes after the same group sued xAI over its use of gas generators without the required permits in an area with more than 100,000 inhabitants. The generators used by xAI are converted by ProEnergy , a Missouri-based outfit that repurposes the unused General Electric turbines that are typically found attached to Boeing airplanes. The company was quick to turn its attention to the possibility of using the jet engines to power data centers after it was identified that the demand for energy was outpacing the ability of traditional utility companies to keep up. Each turbine is capable of producing up to 50 megawatts of electricity. Normally, that would be enough to keep around 15,000 homes up and running. The availability of energy has long been an issue for data centers, both existing and those still on the drawing board. A July 2026 report predicted that data centers would use 20% of all U.S. power by 2035 , a figure that was a huge 83% increase over the same forecast that was made seven months prior. Despite that news, as of April this year, half of data center buildouts had been canceled or delayed due to, among other things, a lack of power. This is an issue for xAI especially, with Musk saying in August that xAI would increase its data center capacity by 7x before the end of 2027. Delays and cancelations have the potential to derail those plans. Public sentiment around data centers has turned sour in recent months amid power issues and concerns over how much water these facilities use. While using converted jet engines could potentially help with one issue, it seems unlikely that the pollution they generate will help assuage the concerns of locals anytime soon.

articles.title: Apple faces unprecedented memory cost increases as RAM prices continue to surge, manufacturing bill climbs by $33 billion
articles.content: Apple is about to feel the squeeze from rising memory prices, with the cost of RAM climbing just as the company heads into its busiest shopping season. According to Reuters , Apple expects to pay more for memory in the December quarter, with the CEO, John Ternus, describing the current price increases as “unprecedented. The company has so far managed to soften the blow by using memory bought at lower prices, cutting costs elsewhere and raising prices on some products. However, it is reported that its manufacturing bill has climbed by $33 billion in just a few months. Go deeper with TH Premium: Memory (Image credit: SK Hynix) AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers The future of DRAM: From DDR5 to future ICs High-bandwidth memory roadmap Inside the history of DRAM price-fixing lawsuits But that cushion is getting thinner, and Apple expects memory purchases to become even more expensive into 2027. “What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset.” Ternus said during Apple’s November 2 earnings call . Memory is used across Apple's hardware lineup, so sustained price increases could affect manufacturing cost for several product categories—although Apple has not announced another round of price increases. Absorbing higher components could, however, indefinitely become difficult. Dave Nicholson, Chief Research Officer at the Futurum Group, also identified memory prices as a growing pressure point for Apple's margins and hardware pricing through the holiday season and into 2027. According to him, Apple is in a different position from companies pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into AI data center infrastructure. The impact of higher component costs is easier to quantify than the eventual returns on massive AI capital expenditure, he said. The next pressure point for @Apple may not be AI CapEx, but the rising cost of memory across its hardware portfolio.@TheFuturumGroup Chief Research Officer @DaveN007 explained that higher memory prices could put more pressure on Apple’s margins and pricing through the holiday season and into 2027. Even with demand holding up, the question is how much of those higher costs consumers will absorb.Dave also sees Apple in a stronger position than companies committing hundreds of billions to data center infrastructure, because the impact of higher component costs is easier to quantify than the long-term returns on massive AI CapEx.▶️ Watch Dave’s analysis of Apple’s margin outlook, memory costs, and why its AI infrastructure strategy could give the company more flexibility.#Apple #AI #Semiconductors #Futurum November 3, 2026 And the warnings from Apple's suppliers suggest that the cost pressure is unlikely to ease quickly. Last month, Samsung , a major supplier of RAM(DRAM), NAND flash storage and OLED displays for Apple, said that memory demand would far exceed supply as AI infrastructure continues to expand. Its memory division also reported a quarter-on-quarter increase in DRAM average prices during the third quarter, while NAND prices rose by high-teen percentages. Senior executive vice president of its memory business warned the supply crunch could extend to 2028 and beyond. Elsewhere, SK Hynix delivered a similar warning, saying it had secured long-term agreements covering more than Half of its production capacity for2027 and 2028. Micron, the third major supplier for Apple aside…

articles.title: Hands-on with the DockCase Mount Ling 2 Pro
articles.content: DockCase is no stranger to Kickstarting unique SSD enclosures and docks, with the company’s Visual Smart M.2 enclosure making its way onto our list of the best SSD enclosures . The Mount Ling 2 Pro , however, is gunning for a spot among the best USB-C docks . It’s a dock for handhelds like the Steam Deck and Switch 2, an external enclosure for an NVMe SSD, and a game capture device, all packaged up in a dock that can show off your handheld and expand your port selection. There are two versions of the dock: the standard Mount Ling 2 and the Pro version. The only difference between them is the internal capture card. The base version is $109 via an early bird deal while the Kickstarter gets underway, and the Pro version is $149. They’ll be priced at $199 and $249, respectively, after the early deals are gone. It’s the world’s first “smart creator dock,” says DockCase, which is partially true. There are other docks that give you additional inputs, a stand, and capture capabilities with a handheld, and at a lower price. The AVerMedia X’TRA GO, for instance, offers all of that for $160 . The differentiator here is the internal M.2 slot that can support up to 4TB of NVMe storage, with points to mount 2280, 2242, and 2230-sized drives. Of course, this external storage only works with platforms that normally support external storage (so, not the Switch or Switch 2). For PC-adjacent handhelds running Windows or Linux, the Mount Ling 2 Pro is an expensive but useful dock that gives you capture, storage, and port expandability in one attractive package. For the Switch and Switch 2 , the usefulness isn’t as clear. You can’t use the SSD with either platform, and Nintendo’s game of whack-a-mole with third-party accessories means a system update could break HDMI passthrough (and, in the process, the capture function of the dock). Mount Ling Dock 2 specifications (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) DockCase says the Mount Ling 2 Pro supports the Steam Deck, ROG Ally, Switch, Switch 2, and “more,” presumably wrapping up other Windows- or Linux-based handhelds like the ROG Ally X Xbox or Lenovo Legion Go S. Switch and Switch 2 are supported, as well, though getting Nintendo’s handheld to connect properly isn’t always smooth. The dock connects to your handheld with a USB 3.2 Gen Type-C connection capable of 10 Gbps, and DockCase includes a small, braided 40 Gbps cable in the box, along with two right-angle connectors. That single connection gives you up to 100W through the USB-C port, along with Gigabit Ethernet, an HDMI 2.0 connection (4K@60Hz), a single USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A port, and a USB 2.0 port. An additional USB-C connection serves as another USB 3.2 Gen 2 port on the Mount Ling 2, while it becomes the capture card output on the Pro model. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Interestingly, there’s also an optical audio output available. Although I don’t suspect most users will put it to use (HDMI transfers audio, as well), it’s a nice fallback if you plan on using the dock with a more elaborate audio setup. It’s a nice bonus, though I would’ve liked a 3.5mm audio jack as well, considering handhelds no longer have access to that connection. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The dock itself is constructed almost entirely of plastic, and holding it in your hands, you can tell it’s filled with more air than hardware. It’s a sizable package at 8.4 x 7 x 3.5 inches. Outside of the shell, there’s a thick layer of firm silicone to rest your handheld on. There are grooves to provide a natural resting place for just about any handheld, as well as a deep central cut that fits the Switch and Switch 2 specifically. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) You can install your SSD at the bottom of the dock, with mounting points for 2280, 2242, and 2230 drives. There's a single 40mm fan internally, as well as venting around the back and side edges, to keep the drive cool. The fan will automatically adjust its speed out of the box, but you’re free to manually adjust the speed…

This design is ideal for precise, agile flight, but it has one major weakness—the drones are highly sensitive to unexpected contact with their surroundings. If they bump into a wall or another obstacle, they can become destabilized or even break apart.
