articles.title: Bambu Lab H3C 3D printer review: A nine-tool monster
articles.content: The Bambu Lab H3C is the printer we’ve been waiting for: a true Bambu tool changer. It has nine “Swaptek” tools that use a technology similar to the H2C Vortek rack, except each nozzle is built into a lightweight, hardwired tool with a dedicated filament path. The H3C is Bambu’s fastest multicolor 3D printer, and though it reduces waste, it does not eliminate it. The H3C comes with a surprising “old school” technology: the ability to print 2.85mm filament. This is in response to China’s increasing fascination with 3D-printed shoes made with a wide variety of squishy TPU. Bambu sent along a few spools of their new super soft 75A TPU to show off, and it does make for comfy footwear. Each unit comes with one special 2.85mm tool as a standard feature, though you can buy a “normal” 1.75mm tool for $59 if you’re not into the novelty of phat filament. You will also be able to add cutting, drawing, embossing, and foil transfer tools to the system. These were not available at the time of review, but we’ve seen these accessories on the H2D and A2L . The 3D printer will NOT come with a laser variant. Bambu is checking off yet another item from the user wish list: the ability to print with more than one nozzle size. Because this is more of a software upgrade, you’ll also gain the ability to mix nozzles with Bambu’s other dual nozzle systems: the H2D, H2C , and X2D . The H2D will get the ability first, and the other printers will be updated by March. The H3C has a 330 x 320 x 325mm build volume (the same as the H2C) and a massive “AMS” type module perched atop the main unit that holds nine spools. This gives it a somewhat towering mushroom shape that’s over three feet tall. It did not fit on my studio counter, which is a standard-sized IKEA kitchen countertop with a filament rack three feet off the surface. When we parked it on my industrial-grade shelving unit next to the H2D, even my 6’4” husband needed a step stool to load filament. Bambu was prepared for this problem and created a special rolling cart for the machine to make it more accessible. This is the first time the company has offered custom furniture for one of their printers and is an optional purchase that I highly recommend. H2C and H3C, side by side. (Image credit: Bambu Lab) All nine tools are integrated into the bottom of the AMS 3H, which means the H3C only comes as a nine-tool 3D printer. There is no such thing as a single-color H3C. If nine colors aren’t enough for you, the printer can be hooked up to as many as four “normal” AMS units with the help of an optional buffer. Unfortunately, all outside AMS units need to run through the 5th tool slot, so you will lose the purge-free perk of the H3C. The AMS 3H does not have motorized rollers, as retraction is unneeded on a tool changer. Seven of the slots have a TPU bypass, something we first saw on the single spool AMS HT . Two of the slots are nestled within an interior chamber for drying at up to 85°C. Though you can only dry two spools in the AMS 3H, you can run the dryer while printing, as it has its own power supply. The sealed dryer does not “leak” enough heat to dry the rest of the chamber…we checked. But that also means you don’t have to worry about the dryer melting a spool of PLA left in a nearby slot. The FlexFeed extruder mounted on the toolhead is amazing. It can self-adjust to handle normal 1.75mm PLA or expand to push 2.85mm TPU quickly and without issue. The Bambu Lab H3C comes standard with eight .4mm nozzles for 1.75mm filament and one .4mm nozzle for 2.85mm filament. The nozzles are held in place with three screws and are pretty easy to swap out. You do need an entirely separate tool (with larger openings) for the 2.85mm filament. Because the H3C can print with multiple nozzle sizes, you could leave one or more tools dedicated to .2, .6, or .8 nozzle sizes if that fits your workflow. For example, slots 6 and 8 are located inside the dryer and have a TPU bypass. You could dedicate a .6mm nozzle to these…

articles.title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
articles.content: You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished. AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure. To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire : a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next. How it works Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section. Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it. We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer. Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops. Our focus Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation. We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions. A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements. A walk through Zero Wire Start on the Zero Wire homepage . Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer. Find what needs attention The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system…

articles.title: Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same.
articles.content: Anthropic has announced a new feature that aims to speed up long-running Claude Code sessions by reducing the amount of conversation data repeatedly sent to its API, helping developers get responses faster as their coding sessions grow. Message threads , as it’s called, is available now in public beta for Anthropic’s Messages API and is already enabled by default for “most” Claude Code users, according to an article published by Anthropic on Monday. The company says that the feature has reduced median time to first token (TTFT) — the time it takes Claude to begin generating a response — by approximately 35% for Claude Code requests containing between 500,000 and 1 million tokens. Given that it’s now part of the Messages API, the feature also extends beyond Claude Code to developers building their own AI agents, particularly those handling lengthy conversations, repeated tool calls, and large amounts of data. How message threads works To understand what’s changed, it’s worth looking at how the Messages API has traditionally handled conversations. Every time an agent sends a new request to Claude, it includes the entire conversation history. That means all messages and tool calls must be transmitted again, even though the API has previously received them. For example, a coding agent working through a complex task will likely entail hundreds of API calls. As it reads files and modifies code, the conversation history grows, and by the time that history reaches 500,000 tokens, every subsequent request requires sending those 500,000 tokens again, along with whatever new information has been thrown into the mix. The API then has to validate and tokenize the incoming data before Claude can begin responding. This rinse-and-repeat processing can add significant latency, particularly during lengthy coding sessions. And so message threads switches things up by allowing Anthropic to temporarily retain the conversation history on its servers. The first request still sends the complete conversation, including any system prompts and tool definitions. But subsequent requests need only contain new messages and a reference to the previous response. Behind the scenes, Anthropic reconstructs the full conversation on its servers before passing it to Claude, negating the need for the client to keep uploading the same information. This detail is important, because Claude still processes the entire conversation on every turn — if the history contains 500,000 tokens, the model still receives that context, even though the client has transmitted only the latest messages. “While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.” As such, message threads doesn’t inherently reduce API costs — Anthropic continues to charge for the tokens Claude processes. “While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same,” the company notes. Developers can, however, combine message threads with Claude’s existing prompt caching feature , which allows previously processed content to be reused at discounted token rates. The two features can work in tandem to reduce latency and processing costs respectively. Anthropic identifies several use-cases where message threads could be particularly useful. These include long-running coding agents that accumulate file edits and tool results, computer-use agents that repeatedly capture screenshots, and applications handling large volumes of documents or images. In each case, avoiding repeated uploads reduces the amount of data transmitted during a session. articles.title: Nvidia tells data center operators to limit business from Chinese customers with new global restrictions, report claims
articles.content: Nvidia has purportedly told its data center customers that they must limit the amount of business that they do with Chinese companies in what is a new policy for the U.S. company. The move would mean that data center operators who sell their services to Chinese companies must now track what proportion of their overall business they make up, limiting them to just 49% of the total and ensuring 51% are non-Chinese outfits. The FT reports the new policy has been communicated to Nvidia's customers by its sales force and regional teams, and does not appear to have been laid out in any official form via documentation. Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained Notably, Nvidia's alleged new stance on Chinese customers does not only apply to data centers that are located in Asia. Instead, it applies to those based globally, and even then it only affects new and future contracts rather than any existing Nvidia hardware leasing agreements that are in place. In a statement, Nvidia notes that "American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide." The statement goes on to say that current U.S. policy "encourages" cloud providers to build on American infrastructure and to accept business from "everywhere they can." But this latest move to restrict Chinese access to Nvidia's high-performance data center hardware comes amid ongoing tensions between the United States and China with regard to AI capabilities. Nvidia can only sell its chips to whitelisted companies , a situation that has led to a thriving black market for its wares. Earlier this year, it was found that even Nvidia's older servers have become so sought-after that their values have tripled. Whether limitations on who Nvidia can sell its chips to have had the desired effect is open to debate, with even China's state-owned telecoms giant China Telecom having recently been found to have Nvidia hardware in its data centers . The situation wouldn't be out of place in a blockbuster espionage thriller, with Nvidia CEO Jason Huang reportedly the target of a spy plot by Chinese agents . The reasons behind the U.S. government's attempts to limit China's access to Nvidia hardware are obvious. The aim is to stymie China's ability to advance its own AI technologies, with Nvidia chips the go-to option for AI servers and data centers around the globe. But this limitation on which customers cloud service providers can accept will put additional strain on companies that are already fighting it out for the same contracts. Reducing the pool of potential customers could potentially see a shrinking in the scale of data center operations moving forward.

articles.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal. Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice. Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave . —Amit Katwala Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.” But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks. So one month in, who’s on board? —James O’Donnell This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. articles.title: China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October
articles.content: Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek . The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion. The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding. Funding concentration Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital , Index Ventures and Lux Capital . DeepSeek ’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance , and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI . DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI , a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board . The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity. Other large rounds last month went to Axiom , which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp , which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent , which says it raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi , which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes , which raised a $1 billion Series A. AI-driven A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI , which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev. A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month. Exits The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX ’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion . On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber ’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion. Looking ahead With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds. articles.title: Cops Bust Botnet of 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes
articles.content: A coalition of security firms working with Japan's National Police Agency has disrupted a botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices across 200+ countries. "We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology," the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a blog post. The Register reports: Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. The firmware's pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation. The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. "Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to GTIG. Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
articles.content: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood. A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms). Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically. The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer. A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says. During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. articles.title: AI wearables want to remember everything. What happens when we can’t forget?
articles.content: A growing number of companies are pitching AI hardware products as a remedy for one of humanity’s oldest weaknesses: forgetfulness. The latest such product comes from Amazon, whose Bee subsidiary introduced a $75 wristband called the Bee Frontier last month. The band, which looks a little like a screen-free fitness tracker, can record meetings and other conversations using two built-in microphones. Frontier owners can then access transcripts and conversation summaries on their phones or computers. Amazon is also getting ready to sell a Bee phone accessory to keep track of your calls. The company’s pitch for these devices is that they will help you keep track of the many details that would otherwise fall by the wayside, all while safeguarding your privacy with encryption. Amazon isn’t the only company looking to capture your work and family conversations. In September, Apple unveiled a new feature called Siri Recap for the latest Apple Watch models that can summarize conversations the watch listens in on. A new smart glasses brand called Vonder wants to keep track of your side of every conversation. And a number of work-centric AI recording devices promise to keep track of all your in-office conversations. To be sure, these gadgets raise privacy concerns. But beyond the fear that any single conversation may be listened in on, there’s a bigger question to consider with the emergence of such devices: How will human interactions change if every word we utter may get sucked up by an AI-powered microphone, to be preserved for eternity? [Photo: Meta] LED lights alone don’t make devices privacy-friendly To its credit, Amazon has been trying to address privacy concerns related to Bee products head-on. Audio captured by the devices is processed in real time and then immediately deleted. Transcripts and summaries are processed and stored in an encrypted private compute environment that even Amazon’s own employees can’t access. And any time a Bee device is used to capture a conversation, an LED turns on. A number of other AI wearables, including Meta’s Ray-Ban AI glasses, also rely on LEDs to signal recording activity to bystanders. But privacy advocates argue that these lights are insufficient. “That LED light might be known to some people to signify that a camera or a microphone is on and is being used, but not necessarily to every person,” says Electronic Privacy Information Center senior counsel Sara Geoghegan. “It’s small, and people might not notice it.” Things can get especially dicey in states like California and Florida, which have two-party consent laws that make it illegal to record private conversations without the consent of other participants. Simply having a device signal that it is recording may not be enough to record others legally in those states. “I don’t think that a small LED light on someone’s glasses across from you is consent,” Geoghegan says. What’s more, some Ray-Ban users have tampered with their LEDs to record others without their knowledge. This reportedly led Meta to remotely disable thousands of glasses. By and large, companies rely on users of their devices to notify bystanders that they’re being recorded. That can be harder than it sounds, even for well-meaning owners. “Consent is perhaps impossible, if not much more difficult, to obtain from a crowd of people,” Geoghegan argues. AI recorders could erode public spaces Not everyone is as worried about the ability of these devices to record people without their knowledge. “I think consent is overvalued,” says Oxford University professor Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, who is instead more concerned about the broader impact of pervasive, AI-powered recording. “The ephemerality of public spaces has evaporated,” he warns. People used to be able to go to a museum or a bar without worrying that anything and everything they said might get recorded and analyzed. “There used to be a sort of built-in forgetting in public spaces,” Mayer-Schönberger…

articles.title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
articles.content: Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch. This was what it looked like before you made the change: The selector matches more than we meant. The :has(img) rule matches any descendant image, so the comment’s avatar counted as a hero image. And the p element selector matches any descendant paragraph. As a result, the comment’s text was caught in the selection. The selector outweighed the comment’s own rule. MDN’s specificity guide explains that :has() adds no weight by itself, but its argument does. That gives .card:has(img) p a specificity score of 0-1-2, while .comment p comes in at just 0-1-1 and loses the battle. It could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that says “spacing looks off sometimes.” The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators: .card:has(> img) > p { margin: 0; } This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about. Nesting Also Borrows Weight Native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity says the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is() . Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example : /* Specificity 1-0-0 */ .card, #featured { /* Specificity: 1-0-1 */ & a { color: blue; } } /* Specificity: 0-1-0 */ .button { color: red; } A .button link inside a .card is blue , even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared. The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where() : /* :where() always weighs 0-0-0 */ :where(.card, #featured) { /* Specificity: 0-0-1 */ & a { color: blue; } } /* Specificity: 0-1-0 */ .button { color: red; } Plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate. Layers Don’t Rescue You By Default Don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your new component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !important keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order. Miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head. An Old Fight With A New Tool None of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?” , one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade: “Here’s a fun one: refactoring your JS can cause your CSS to break, because your CSS builds are determined by JS import orders.” — mq2thez This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. articles.title: Zoomtopia 2026: Zoom Got It Done! Maybe…
articles.content: “Zoom Got It Done” is the tagline for the company’s new Zoom Ahead campaign, with the focus being how Zoom’s AI-first capabilities take conversations to completion. This one features Kate McKinnon and builds on their “I Use Zoom!” spot with Bowen Yang that kicked off this consumer-friendly campaign late last year. For the record, I’m not a fan of their comedic approach here, but the ads hold your attention, and it’s great seeing SNL favorites playing over-the-top corporate tropes. Am just not so sure the messaging gets it done. Wearing my Marketing hat, I’ll note that B2C marketing campaigns from tech companies are really hard to do well, especially when the audience is not the economic buyer. The Zoom ads are aimed at workers – end users – while the buyers – IT and CEOs – are caricatured as the worker’s worst nightmare. This is a topic I’d love to explore further, but I need to stay on script and tie their Got It Done tagline to the main topic, namely my review of the recent Zoomtopia event. While the event is mainly for customers and partners, I was part of the small cohort of analysts who attended as well. Since Zoomtopia caters primarily to those economic buyers, it wasn’t surprising that the Got It Done message was the opening theme for the event, capped by a local choir that went full gospel to celebrate the uplifting power of AI to get work done and relieve us of so many tedious tasks that undermine our productivity. Am not sure if everyday workers get that euphoria when using Zoom, but that’s the aspiration – nothing wrong with that, amen. Choir singing the praises of ‘Got It Done’ Jon Arnold More importantly, I think Zoom is trying to communicate how AI is transforming their platform into something bigger than video calls and meetings. On that count, I think Zoomtopia succeeded, perhaps in ways that most people don’t realize. In that context (pun intended), I’ve distilled my takeaways into three big ideas. 1. Unified Context Layer This was the big story at the event, so let’s start there. I’m never the first analyst to post about industry events, but I’m going with flow here, as this was the lede most of my peers went with for their write-ups. What I haven’t seen so far, though, is connecting the dots to the last time most of our group was at a Zoom event. That would be Perspectives, their analyst-only event, and back in April we got the deep dive on their go-to-market vision, “from conversation to completion”. The overall reception was positive, and it marked a new chapter in Zoom’s evolution to align more closely with AI’s transformative potential and get beyond being a meetings platform. Building on the premise that all interactions start with some form of conversation, AI does all the hard work of taking those conversational inputs, identifying next-best actions and closing with intelligent task completion. At Zoomtopia 2026, the big story was Unified Context Layer, which takes that vision one step further. The missing piece was context, where AI is now better able to understand intent, sentiment, urgency, etc., and connect all that to memory across the entire lifecycle of an interaction. Humans simply cannot do this at scale and in real time, so this is where the AI story becomes next level. On a more basic level, this is no longer about human-to-human communication, the foundation upon which all UCaaS platforms are built. Communication remains the cornerstone for how work gets done, but now it’s just as much about P2P as it is about P2A, A2P, A2A and B2B. Translation – people need to communicate among themselves, but increasingly it’s also agent-to-agent, bot-to-bot and everything in between. Getting context right is more challenging when AI agents are involved, and that point will tie into my second big theme. articles.title: Apple Released the iPhone X Nine Years Ago Today
articles.content: Apple's iPhone X went on sale nine years ago today, November 3, 2017. The 10th-anniversary iPhone was the first with an all-screen OLED display and no Home button, and its gesture navigation and Face ID authentication shaped the flagship iPhone models that followed it. Announced on September 12, 2017 , the iPhone X used its TrueDepth camera to introduce Face ID, which replaced Touch ID on the device. Powered by the A11 Bionic chip, it was also Apple's first iPhone to start at $999. Apple classified the device as vintage in 2024 . Recently, Touch ID made an unlikely return to iPhones with the iPhone Duo. Apple is expected to introduce a redesigned 20th-anniversary iPhone in late 2027. This article, " Apple Released the iPhone X Nine Years Ago Today " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Nudify apps are hiding in plain sight on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store
articles.content: TL;DR Researchers uncovered a network of over 400 ‘nudify’ apps and websites on the Play Store and App Store. These apps masquerade as innocent tools and reveal a hidden deepfake interface after installation. The apps were traced back to Chinese developers and Hong Kong-based KeLing Technology Limited. Apple and Google often talk about the strict guidelines that apps need to follow in order to be allowed on their stores. However, every few months, new reports emerge of harmful apps making their way onto both the Play Store and the App Store. Apps like the fake Chrome browser spotted last month are concerning enough, but Google and Apple have a much bigger, more alarming problem on their hands with “nudify” apps. Earlier this year, around 38 “nudify” apps were found on the App Store and Play Store , accounting for a combined 483 million downloads and $122 million in revenue. Now, Wired has uncovered that there may be several hundred more. What’s worse is that they are now masquerading as innocent services, such as language tutoring, AI-based pet photo editing, and workout coaching apps.
articles.author: Akshay Gangwar
articles.fingerprint: app apple apps google hiding nudify plain play sight store

articles.title: The espresso machine I recommend to all beginners is $200 off right now — the same price as Black Friday
articles.content: I've tested well over 50 coffee machines now. Manuals, bean-to-cups, superautomatics — even the lever Flair 49 Pro (yes, no electricity involved at all). But which is the ultimate best espresso machine... for beginners? I would recommend something with a built-in grinder. While some people will tell you machines with built-in grinders are inherently inferior, I disagree. A "good" grinder can set you back hundreds of dollars — on top of your espresso machine. This can easily make your coffee setup almost a thousand dollars... and that's before the actual coffee beans. So if you want your first espresso machine but you're not sure which one to get, let me help you out. I'd recommend the Breville Barista Express , which we awarded 4.5 stars in our review, and it remains a classic. And the best part? It's currently just $499 at Amazon — yes, the same price as the Breville Bambino Plus . So you're really getting that grinder for free. The Barista Express remains one of the most popular and recommended espresso machines for a reason. Like every other Breville, it has a PID controller (although unadjustable, but better than no PID controller!), a powerful steam wand, and a built in grinder. View Deal Why is the Breville Barista Express so good for beginners? (Image credit: Tom's Guide) One reason: convenience. The Breville Barista Express is easy to use, making it ideal for newer home baristas. While you still need to dial in beans yourself, this is a skill all baristas should dedicate time to learning — and you'll notice your espresso tastes so much better once you've figured it out. Your espresso should pour like honey . Like every other Breville, the Barista Express has a PID controller, which means the machine controls your water temperature at every stage of the brewing process. I would personally never buy an espresso machine without a PID controller (or similar). This ensures your espresso is never burned or weak, but just right. You can also customize pre-infusion time: this is where you soak the grounds with water at low pressure, extracting nuanced and delicate flavors, before ramping up the pressure for a full extraction. But you also don't have to use this feature — you can just press the "shot" button and espresso will come out. So while the Breville Barista Express has a range of enthusiast features like adjustable pre-infusion and a PID controller, it also has a built-in grinder and easy-to-use steam wand. This machine will grow with you, from your early days of Googling things like: "What is espresso???" all the way to your serious barista era. It's the Goldilocks of coffee, so to speak. And because the Bambino Plus is $499 full price, you're kind of getting the built-in Baratza grinder for free. articles.content: Credit: Ryan Haines / Android Authority TL;DR Google Vids now lets you create custom avatars using just photos. While you can just edit videos on a typical timeline, Gemini adds a lot more features, including the options to turn Docs or Slides into videos , edit videos with simple text-based prompts , and even transform how people in the videos look. Besides video editing, Vids also lets you generate human-looking (or human-inspired) characters using AI , with options to customize characteristics such as age, gender, race, and more. Now, Google is adding more options to customize the avatar and make it resemble you. Google is now adding an option in the Vids app that lets you create custom avatars using just images. Previously, users were required to go through the entire process of creating an avatar in Gemini using Google’s likeness tool . The latter required scanning your face from different angles and recording your voice.

articles.title: Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights
articles.content: The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow. But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona . Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior. "We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post . "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly." To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math. Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold. There was no training using gradient descent ; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights. "All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post . "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming. "Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights." Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so. Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting , which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge. More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment. The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say. ®
articles.author: Thomas Claburn

articles.content: TL;DR OpenAI is expanding the AI models powering ChatGPT Dots, including GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Terra. Dots will automatically choose the best AI model for each task and can use multiple models to get the job done. GPT-6.1 Terra promises faster performance and a friendlier personality, while helping OpenAI bring Dots to more users. OpenAI is making ChatGPT Dots more capable, but the interesting part isn’t just that they’re getting access to more powerful AI models. It’s that they’ll be able to choose the right model for whatever you’re asking, so you won’t have to figure that out yourself. Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, shared on X that the company is expanding the lineup of models powering Dots. This includes GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Terra , with more expected to arrive down the road. According to Sottiaux, Terra brings faster performance and a more pleasant personality, while also helping OpenAI make Dots available to more people.

articles.content: You might tell ChatGPT things you’d never share with a stranger. Maybe you’ve asked it about a medical concern, argued with your spouse in a conversation about relationship advice or uploaded a document containing financial information. But before your next conversation, here's something to know: Real people at AI companies may be able to read some of what you share. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic all have policies that allow certain conversations to be reviewed by humans, whether to improve their AI systems, investigate potential safety violations or troubleshoot problems. That doesn’t mean someone is sitting behind a screen reading every message you send, but the assumption that your AI conversations are strictly between you and the chatbot is not accurate. Not to mention, just deleting a conversation doesn’t always mean the company deletes every copy immediately. In Google’s case, Gemini chats reviewed by humans can remain in company systems for up to three years, even after you delete your activity. Here’s what actually happens to your conversations, who might be able to read them and what you can do to protect your privacy. Yes, humans can read some AI conversations (Image credit: Getty Images/Kelly Sikkema) When you type a question into ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, your message is typically sent to the company’s servers, where an AI model processes it and generates a response. Most of that process is automated. But AI companies also use human reviewers to evaluate certain conversations. Several reasons might prompt a review; safety is a big one. AI companies use automated systems to detect potentially harmful requests, policy violations and suspicious activity. Some interactions may be escalated for human review. Another reason conversations are reviewed is for improving the AI itself. Depending on your settings and the company’s policies, selected conversations may be used to evaluate responses, identify mistakes and help improve future models. Companies generally describe measures intended to protect users during these reviews, including limiting access and removing identifying information. But removing a person’s name or account details doesn’t necessarily remove every sensitive fact contained in a conversation. For example, a chat about a medical diagnosis , workplace dispute or financial problem could contain personal information even without the user’s name attached. The important difference is that human review doesn’t happen to every conversation, and the rules vary depending on which chatbot you’re using. What big tech might do with your conversations ChatGPT (Image credit: Shutterstock) OpenAI allows consumer ChatGPT conversations to be used to improve its models unless users opt out. You can disable this by opening Settings > Data Controls and turning off Improve the model for everyone . But disabling training doesn’t mean every conversation becomes inaccessible to human reviewers. OpenAI’s Data Controls FAQ explains that Temporary Chats aren’t used for training but may be reviewed to monitor abuse. Temporary Chats also don’t appear in your regular chat history and are generally deleted from OpenAI’s systems after 30 days. For ordinary saved conversations, OpenAI says deleting a chat removes it from your account immediately and schedules it for permanent deletion within 30 days, unless the information has already been de-identified or must be retained for legal or security reasons. Google Gemini (Image credit: Shutterstock) Google is particularly explicit about how human reviewers may access conversations. According to Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub , some conversations are reviewed by humans to improve its services and help protect users. Google says conversations sent to service providers for review are disconnected from users’ accounts before being examined. But there’s a significant catch: Chats reviewed by humans can be retained for up to three years, and deleting your Gemini Apps activity…

articles.title: Latest Snapseed update gives you a few more reasons to skip Lightroom
articles.content: TL;DR Snapseed v4.2 is gradually rolling out on Android and iOS. The update adds support for importing presets and LUTs, sharing custom Looks with their LUTs, browsing community Looks, and a depth-based mode for Lens Blur. It also brings the Motion Blur tool from iPhone to Android, along with full multi-wheel Color Grading. As a longtime Snapseed fan, I was stoked when Google finally started showing the app some love this year. Since then, the company has rolled out several new features and improved the app in multiple ways. Well, it doesn’t seem like Google is planning to stop anytime soon. Google has started rolling out Snapseed v4.2 on Android and iOS, and the update introduces several new features to the much-loved photo-editing app (via Droid Life ). The update brings the Motion Blur tool—previously only available on iPhones—to Android users as well.

articles.title: Ridley Scott’s $100M box office flop might secretly be his best movie — and you can stream it free on Tubi
articles.content: Get people to name Ridley Scott’s best movie and you’ll hear “Gladiator,” “Alien” or “Blade Runner,” but one of his finest in recent years is a film almost nobody saw in theaters. That movie is “The Last Duel,” a brutal, brilliant medieval drama from 2021 that flopped hard on release, but is getting its second wind on streaming thanks to platforms like Tubi. Directed by Scott and based on Eric Jager’s book, “The Last Duel” dramatizes the true story of the last legally sanctioned duel to the death in medieval France. It tells the same events three times, “Rashomon”-style, from three different points of view, with the final version belonging to the woman at the center of it all. It pulled in just $30 million at the box office against a $100 million budget, but critics admired it, and in the years since it’s come to be regarded as one of Scott’s best films. Now that it's streaming free on Tubi, there's no excuse not to give one of the most underrated movies of the decade the attention it always deserved. What is 'The Last Duel' about? J ean de Carrouges (Matt Damon) and Jacques Le Gris (Adam Driver) are close friends in 14th-century France, two men who once fought side by side in battle. But they couldn’t be more different. Carrouges is a proud, hot-tempered knight who feels the world owes him more than it’s given him, while Le Gris is charming, educated and quick to rise in the favor of their powerful lord, Count Pierre d’Alençon (Ben Affleck). As Le Gris climbs and Carrouges keeps getting passed over for lands and titles he believes are rightfully his, their friendship devolves into a rivalry. Things escalate further when Carrouges marries Marguerite (Jodie Comer), a strong-willed noblewoman. While Carrouges is away, Le Gris forces his way into their home and assaults her. When her husband returns, Marguerite does something extraordinarily dangerous for a woman of her time: She refuses to stay silent, naming Le Gris as her attacker. Enraged and determined to defend his wife’s honor, Carrouges petitions the king for a trial by combat, a duel to the death in which God is said to grant victory to whoever is telling the truth. Why I recommend streaming 'The Last Duel' "The Last Duel" is an interesting mix of both rage and spectacle. I went in expecting a straightforward medieval epic, so I was surprised to realize it had a lot to say about truth and power dynamics — and, of course, believing women at its heart. (Image credit: Tubi) As a "Rashomon" fan, the movie's three-perspective structure is what actually elevates it. Watching the exact same events replay from Jean’s self-serving point of view, then Jacques’s, then Marguerite’s, you start to notice how casually these men rewrite their own histories, and how differently a woman experiences the same moments the men barely register. Matt Damon and Adam Driver are both excellent as the two rivals, Ben Affleck is a surprising addition I didn't see coming, and Jodie Comer is fantastic as Marguerite. And in the end, the final duel is one of the most viscerally intense sequences Scott has ever put to film. If you're wondering about how it might leave you mentally when the credits roll, you can just sit with it at home to reckon with those feelings. Whatever the case, you should absolutely give it a watch, as you'll want to make sure you catch it while it's streaming free. Stream "The Last Duel" free on Tubi now

articles.title: T-Mobile’s fastest internet plan yet comes with a surprising 10-year promise
articles.content: TL;DR T-Mobile is launching a 5Gbps fiber plan for $90/month with a 10-year price guarantee. Limited-time deals include free service months and up to $300 in prepaid cards. The guarantee only covers the top tier. Your internet provider wants you to think bigger is always better. T-Mobile is making that pitch with a new 5Gbps fiber plan, but the more intriguing number isn’t the speed. It’s the ten years the carrier says customers can keep paying the same base rate. Starting November 3, T-Mobile Fiber 5 Gig costs $90 a month with AutoPay, plus taxes and fees. That’s cheaper than AT&T’s $125 standalone 5Gbps rate announced earlier this year, and even its $100 bundled price. T-Mobile doesn’t require a wireless subscription to qualify.

articles.titleFa: T-Mobile، طرح اینترنتی جدید با سرعت بالا و وعده‌ای عجیب به مدت ۱۰ سال را معرفی کرد
articles.summaryFa: T-Mobile به تازگی یک طرح اینترنت فیبر نوری با سرعت ۵ گیگابیت بر ثانیه را با قیمت ۹۰ دلار در ماه و تضمین قیمت برای مدت ۱۰ سال معرفی کرده است. این طرح با تخفیف‌های ویژه شامل ماه‌های رایگان و کارت‌های پیش‌پرداخت تا ۳۰۰ دلار نیز همراه است.
articles.summaryEn: T-Mobile has announced a new 5Gbps fiber plan priced at $90 per month with a 10-year price guarantee. The plan also includes limited-time offers such as free service months and up to $300 in prepaid cards, making it a competitive option in the market.
insightsFa: طرح جدید T-Mobile با سرعت ۵ گیگابیت بر ثانیه، یک رقیب جدی برای AT&T محسوب می‌شود.
تضمین قیمت برای مدت ۱۰ سال می‌تواند جذابیت بالایی برای مشتریان ایجاد کند.
تخفیف‌های ویژه برای مشتریان جدید، تنوع بیشتری به این طرح می‌دهد.
articles.whyItMattersFa: این خبر به دلیل معرفی یک طرح اینترنتی با سرعت بالا و قیمت ثابت برای یک دوره طولانی، می‌تواند تاثیر زیادی بر تصمیم‌گیری کاربران برای انتخاب ارائه‌دهندگان خدمات اینترنتی داشته باشد.
